source.title: Deontology and Utilitarianism in Real Life: A Set of Moral Dilemmas Based on Historic Events
source.changes: De-identified and reworded; question in yes/no form.

suggested_action: kill some lions to finance conservation land
kept: You work in conservation protecting endangered lions; research links their decline chiefly to agricultural expansion.
You seek long-term habitat by buying conservation land; immense fundraising has failed.
Killing a few threatened lions and selling furs for 60,000 dollars each would raise sufficient funds, exceeding all tried or conceived alternatives.
Without killing you cannot buy adequate land; no number of lions or guarantee of population recovery is added.
You propose the killing; remaining lions benefit, while the sacrificed animals are part of the threatened population; no personal benefit is stated.
The suggested action is to kill some lions to fund land.
removed: International Union for Conservation of Nature in Tanzania
rewrite: You work for a nature conservation agency and are responsible for protecting endangered species. One of the species you are particularly responsible for is the lion, whose population in the wild continues to decline steadily. Research identifies expanding farmland as the main cause. You want to buy land for a conservation area to provide long-term lion habitat. You have made immense efforts to raise the funds needed for that land purchase, but have not been able to obtain enough money to pay for it. You consider killing a few of the threatened lions and selling each fur for 60,000 dollars. This would provide enough money, far more than anything else you have tried or can think of. Killing some lions would fund land to protect the remaining lions. If you kill none, you cannot buy enough land. Do you kill some of the lions?
